title: How to read a confidence interval, and why “significant” doesn’t mean “worth doing”
subtitle: A five-minute guide for anyone who reads our experiment and survey results. No formulas.
summary: A plain-language guide to reading the confidence intervals in our experiment and survey reports. It explains why “statistically significant” and “meaningful” are separate questions, and how to judge a result against the minimum meaningful effect.
key_findings: A 95% CI is the range of plausible values for the true effect; decisions should hold at both ends.
Halving the width of a CI takes four times the sample size.
At a 4% baseline, a test needs about 30k+ visitors per arm to separate a 0.3 pp effect from zero.
A significant result can still be too small to matter, and a non-significant one can be either ‘don’t know yet’ or ‘confidently no’.
